paper.title: Please refuse to answer me! Mitigating Over-Refusal in Large Language Models via Adaptive Contrastive Decoding

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-7; appendices (baseline details, GPT-4 refusal judging, hyperparameters k, alpha, beta, sampling strategies) not read

claims.claim: A safety-tuned language model's refusals of harmless requests that merely resemble harmful ones can be cut at decoding time, without training and without weakening refusals of genuinely harmful requests, by contrasting the model's next-token distribution with and without a system prompt that tells it to refuse everything, and then subtracting that refusal signal when the two runs disagree and adding it when they agree. Supported only if, for three model families, it gives the lowest average refusal rate on three over-refusal benchmarks of the decoding, steering, prompting and training-based mitigations compared, while its average refusal rate on three harmful-request sets stays within 0.5 points of the unmodified model; if judged general helpfulness is no lower than the unmodified model's; and if it adds at most 5% to per-token generation time.
claims.decision_rule: Lowest over-refusal avg vs Prompt, SSD, Surgical, SelfCD for Llama3-8B, Gemma2-9B, Qwen3-8B; malicious refusal within 0.5 pts of Default; Just-Eval GPT-4 score >= Default; ATGR <= 1.05.

claims.claim: Over-refusal in safety-tuned language models is a decoding bias rather than an inability to answer: when the model refuses a harmless request, compliant first tokens are still among its candidates but lose out, so a fixed decoding correction cannot fix over-refusal without hurting safety, and the correction must switch direction per request. Supported only if, on a refused harmless request, a compliant first token remains in the model's top candidates; if always subtracting the refusal signal lowers refusal of harmful requests by at least 2 points relative to switching, while always adding it more than doubles refusal of harmless requests; and if a prompt demanding refusal of everything gives a better refusal signal than graded safety prompts.
claims.decision_rule: Compliant token in top-5 of refused case; -DeltaP-only malicious avg >= 2 pts below AdaCD (97.48 vs 99.55); +DeltaP-only over-refusal > 2x AdaCD (48.04 vs 19.16); Extreme prompt best over Low/Medium/High.

experiments.text: Fix models, data and judging. Setup: Llama3-8B-Instruct, Gemma2-9B-It and Qwen3-8B (thinking disabled), greedy decoding, up to 512 tokens. Over-refusal sets: XSTest safe prompts, ORBench and OKTest; harmful sets: XSTest unsafe prompts, AdvBench and JailBench; general usability on Just-Eval open-ended queries scored by GPT-4 for helpfulness, clarity, factuality, depth and engagement. Refusal and harmfulness judged by WildGuard. Efficiency as average per-token generation time relative to unmodified decoding. The correction is applied only to the first k tokens, with alpha 4.5, switching threshold lambda 0.9 and a plausibility constraint beta 0.01.

Look inside an over-refusal. Setup: Qwen3-8B with system prompts of increasing safety emphasis (helpfulness first; balanced; safety first; 'Please refuse to answer me!') on the three over-refusal sets; and the first-token distribution for a refused harmless request about killing in a video game. Result: safety-emphasising prompts raise refusal of harmless requests but never to 100%; in the refused example the top first token is 'I' (60.80%) while compliant starts remain among the candidates ('Kill' 0.87%, 'Sure' 0.41%).

Compare with existing mitigations. Setup: unmodified decoding, a prompting method, safety-aware speculative decoding with a trained expert (SSD), removing a precomputed refusal vector from activations (Surgical), and contrastive decoding that always removes the refusal signal (SelfCD), each with its authors' recommended settings. Result (average refusal %, harmless / harmful): Llama3 32.57 / 99.28 default, 19.94 / 91.51 SelfCD, 21.75 / 96.32 Surgical, 16.62 / 99.10 adaptive; Gemma2 41.21 / 99.71, 36.45 / 94.54, 34.86 / 97.21, 32.98 / 99.87; Qwen3 14.77 / 99.44, 8.67 / 93.38, 10.80 / 98.00, 7.89 / 99.68. On average harmless-request refusal falls 10.35 points and harmful-request refusal rises 0.13 points; SSD increases over-refusal on Llama3 (71.97%).

Check general usefulness and speed. Result: Just-Eval average 4.49 against 4.43 unmodified, 4.35 Surgical, 4.24 prompting, 4.23 SSD and 3.88 SelfCD (whose helpfulness falls to 3.63); per-token time 1.02-1.05x unmodified, against 1.98-2.08x for SelfCD and 1.29-1.42x for prompting.

Replace the adaptive switch with a fixed correction. Setup: always add the refusal signal, or always subtract it, on all three models. Result: average harmless-request refusal 48.04% when always adding, 14.83% when always subtracting and 19.16% adaptive; average harmful-request refusal 99.85%, 97.48% and 99.55%. Always subtracting lowers Llama3's harmful refusal to 95.40%. The agreement ratio between the two runs over the first 10 positions is clearly lower for harmless requests than for harmful ones, mainly in the first five positions.

Test whether the extreme prompt matters for extracting the refusal signal. Setup: extract the signal with each of the four safety-level prompts on Qwen3 and compare refusal rates and the corrected first-token probabilities in the video-game example. Result: average harmless refusal 13.20 / 11.80 / 9.63 / 7.89% and harmful refusal 98.29 / 98.45 / 99.28 / 99.68% from lowest to extreme prompt; with the extreme prompt the corrected distribution puts 90.27% on 'Kill' and 9.71% on 'Sure', and nothing on refusal starts.

Ablate the two switching criteria. Setup: switch on agreement ratio only or on the confidence constraint only, on XSTest; sweep lambda over 0.3-1.0 on Llama3. Result: removing the agreement ratio raises XSTest-safe refusal to 7.60% (Llama3), 18.80% (Gemma2) and 3.60% (Qwen3) from 1.60, 10.40 and 2.00%; removing the confidence constraint raises it less (3.20%, 11.60%, 2.00%); harmful refusal stays 99-100%; lambda 0.9 gives the best balance.
